author: original (NevaIB)
title: Ecological niches
bigPicture: A niche is a species' whole way of life: where it lives, what it tolerates, and how it gets food. Modes of nutrition vary enormously, feeding adaptations shape predator–prey and plant–herbivore battles, and no two species can share exactly the same niche for long.

keyIdeas.answer: The role of a species in its ecosystem: all its biotic and abiotic interactions that affect growth, survival and reproduction, including how it obtains food.

keyIdeas.cue: Obligate anaerobe vs facultative anaerobe vs obligate aerobe?
keyIdeas.answer: Obligate anaerobes are poisoned by or can't use oxygen and live only without it. Facultative anaerobes respire aerobically when oxygen is present but can survive without it. Obligate aerobes need oxygen to survive.
Plants, algae and several groups of prokaryotes (e.g. cyanobacteria). They are autotrophs using light energy.
The way all animals feed: food is ingested, digested inside the body, absorbed and assimilated. All animals are heterotrophs.
An organism, e.g. Euglena and many ocean plankton protists, that can both photosynthesise and feed heterotrophically. Obligate mixotrophs need both modes; facultative ones can survive on either.
Some fungi and bacteria secrete enzymes onto dead organic matter, digest it outside their cells and absorb the products. They are decomposers.

Archaea are one of the three domains of life and are very diverse: some use light, some oxidise inorganic chemicals, others oxidise carbon compounds to make ATP. No named examples or biochemistry needed.

keyIdeas.cue: How does dentition show diet in hominids?
keyIdeas.answer: Herbivores: large, flat, thick-enamelled molars for grinding tough plants and strong jaw muscles (Paranthropus robustus, with a skull crest for muscle attachment). Omnivores: smaller molars, varied teeth and smaller jaws (Homo sapiens, Homo floresiensis). Diet is deduced from skulls by comparison with living mammals.

keyIdeas.cue: How do herbivores and plants adapt to each other?
keyIdeas.answer: Insects have piercing (aphids) or chewing (caterpillars) mouthparts. Plants defend with thorns, spines, hairs and toxic secondary compounds in leaves and seeds. Some herbivores evolve ways to detoxify these toxins.

keyIdeas.cue: How do predators and prey adapt?
keyIdeas.answer: Chemical (venom in snakes; toxins and warning colours in prey such as poison dart frogs), physical (claws, speed, camouflage, armour), behavioural (pack hunting, ambush; herding, alarm calls, playing dead).

keyIdeas.cue: How do forest plants harvest light?
keyIdeas.answer: Canopy trees grow tall trunks; lianas climb other trees rooted in the ground; epiphytes grow on branches; strangler figs start as epiphytes and send roots down, eventually enclosing the host; shade-tolerant shrubs and herbs on the floor have large, thin leaves rich in chlorophyll.
Fundamental: the full range a species could occupy given its adaptations and tolerance limits. Realised: the smaller part it actually occupies because of competition with other species.
Two species can't share an identical niche indefinitely. Either one is eliminated from the area, or both are restricted to part of their fundamental niche, so each niche is unique.

keyTerms.def: A species' role and interactions in its ecosystem.
Uses both autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition.
Digests dead matter externally and absorbs the products.
Two species can't occupy the same niche indefinitely.

workedExamples.title: Classic competition data
workedExamples.prompt: Two Paramecium species grow well alone. Grown together, one species' population falls to zero after 16 days. Explain.
steps: Alone, each reaches its own carrying capacity.
Together they compete for the same food (same niche).
The more efficient competitor outcompetes the other.
workedExamples.answer: One species is excluded because their niches overlap completely.

misconceptions.wrong: A niche is just where an organism lives.
misconceptions.right: That is the habitat; the niche is its whole role, including food and interactions.
Some are; others photosynthesise, are chemoautotrophs or are pathogens.

misconceptions.wrong: Facultative anaerobes need no oxygen at all.
misconceptions.right: They can survive without it but use it when available.
Both can coexist by narrowing to their realised niches.
